# Spatiotemporal Composability, Explained Interactively

Source: https://pasekpasek.github.io/spatiotemporal-composability/
Author: Paweł Pasek
Explains: A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability — Yifan Shi, Wei Zhang, Tianyi Cui, arXiv:2608.25512 [cs.PL], August 2026
Reference implementation: Cordis (TypeScript), https://github.com/cordiverse

You disable a plugin in your editor and it asks you to restart. Not because the code is still
loaded, but because nobody knows what that plugin changed. This is a runtime that knows.

## 1. Two orthogonal axes

Time: removing a component has to undo everything it did. The mechanism is revertible effects —
every transformation of the context carries its own inverse, and the runtime holds onto it.

Space: a component declares what it needs from its environment, and the runtime manages that
reactively. The mechanism is reactive coeffects — every change to the context is classified against
a component's declaration and drives its activation or deactivation.

An effect is what a component does to its environment. A coeffect is what it requires from it — the
dual notion, familiar from static analysis, lifted here into a runtime mechanism. Ordinary plugin
code has neither property: the author has to remember the inverse of every line, and in practice
leaves behind a leaked listener, a zombie timer, a dead registry entry.

## 2. The runtime

Components declare `inject` (what they require) and `provide` (what they contribute to the shared
service table). Removing a provider cascades through its dependents, deepest dependent first —
nobody writes that teardown order; it falls out of dependency resolution. The inverse stack empties
exactly as far as it filled: no entry survives its owner.

    export const name = 'auth'
    export const inject = ['db'] as const

    export function apply(ctx: Context<{ db: Database }>) {
      // ctx.db is non-null for the entire lifetime of this fiber:
      // if db goes away, the fiber is torn down before it can observe undefined
      ctx.set('auth', new Auth(ctx.db))
    }

This is what classical dependency injection does not do. A container injects once, at construction.
Here the binding is live, it can be withdrawn, and withdrawal is handled as carefully as provision.

## 3. Revertible effects: track and recover

An ordinary context Γ is lifted to a revertible one, ∂Γ = Γ × (Γ → Γ): the current state γ together
with φ, the composition of the inverses of every effect applied so far.

    track(f, g)(γ, φ) = (f(γ), φ ∘ g)
    recover(γ, φ)     = (φ(γ), id)

Order is the whole game — inverses come off in reverse, like a stack. In Cordis this collapses into
a single call; the effect returns its own inverse and the runtime keeps it:

    export function apply(ctx: Context) {
      ctx.effect(() => {
        const timer = setInterval(poll, 1000)
        return () => clearInterval(timer)
      })
      ctx.on('message', onMessage)        // context APIs are tracked already
      ctx.set('db', new Database())
    }

The entire temporal mechanism, stripped of ergonomics, is a stack of functions:

    type Dispose = () => void
    interface Component { apply(ctx: Ctx): void }

    class Ctx {
      private phi: Dispose[] = []                     // φ — accumulated inverses
      private sigma = new Map<string, unknown>()      // Σ — coeffect context
      private watchers = new Map<string, Set<Dispose>>()
      constructor(private bus: EventTarget) {}

      /** track(f, g): run the effect, keep the inverse, hand it back */
      effect(f: () => Dispose): Dispose {
        const g = f()
        // set once, here at registration — but the closure below runs later, and may run
        // more than once: the caller holds it and recover() reaches it too. The first call
        // spends it, every later one is a no-op. Cordis calls this the armed flag; applying
        // an inverse twice would meet a state no application of the effect ever produced.
        let armed = true
        const dispose: Dispose = () => { if (armed) { armed = false; g() } }
        this.phi.push(dispose)
        return dispose
      }

      /** providing a service is itself a revertible effect */
      set(key: string, value: unknown): Dispose {
        return this.effect(() => {
          const had = this.sigma.has(key), prev = this.sigma.get(key)
          this.sigma.set(key, value)
          this.notify(key)
          return () => {
            had ? this.sigma.set(key, prev) : this.sigma.delete(key)
            this.notify(key)
          }
        })
      }

      /** a tracked context API: the caller never writes this inverse */
      on(event: string, fn: () => void): Dispose {
        return this.effect(() => {
          this.bus.addEventListener(event, fn)
          return () => this.bus.removeEventListener(event, fn)
        })
      }

      /** instantiating a component is not a new mechanism — it is one more effect */
      use(component: Component): Dispose {
        return this.effect(() => {
          const child = new Ctx(this.bus)
          component.apply(child)
          return () => child.recover()            // the child's whole stack, as one inverse
        })
      }

      /** recover: φ(γ) — inverses in reverse order */
      recover(): void { while (this.phi.length) this.phi.pop()!() }

      private notify(key: string): void {
        this.watchers.get(key)?.forEach(fn => fn())
      }
    }

Note that set, on and use never touch the stack themselves — all three are built on effect, because
every context-mutating operation reduces to a ctx.effect call.

Every method hands back the inverse it registered, so one effect can be withdrawn on its own without
disturbing the rest. The disposer disarms itself and leaves φ on the way out — firing an inverse
twice would apply it at a state no application of the effect ever produced.

Taking down a whole component is not a matter of reaching into the stack for its entries. recover is
all-or-nothing, which the paper names as one of the two limitations of the bare track/recover model
and is why the calculus moves on to effect functions and iterators. What gives you per-component
teardown instead is nesting: each fiber runs in its own context with its own φ, and installing a
component on a parent is a single effect whose inverse drains the child's entire stack. That is why
use needs no machinery of its own — a component is not a new kind of thing, it is an effect that
happens to own a context.

The paper goes further and models activation as an effect iterator: each step yields a state change,
its inverse and a continuation. That is what makes a half-finished activation revertible, not just a
completed one. It also unifies the effect context and the coeffect context into a single context type
and mediates every effect and coeffect through it — the discipline it calls the context paradigm, and
the source of the observational equivalence up to which two components' effects interleave.

## 4. Fiber lifecycle

A fiber is the runtime instance of a component — its dependencies, its provisions, and its effect
iterator. The calculus is nine rules over four lifecycle states (Inactive, Reloading, Active,
Unloading) plus an empty node for a fiber absent from the registry. O- rules are actions the
orchestrator may take, their premises saying when the action is legal rather than when it happens;
L- rules are steps the system takes unprompted whenever their premises hold.

    O-Insert   ∅         → Inactive    orchestrator registers the fiber
    O-Retire   any state               raises the retirement flag; carries out nothing itself
    O-Remove   Inactive  → ∅           drops the entry — only once retired, Inactive,
                                       provisioning nothing, and parent to no fiber
    L-Begin    Inactive  → Reloading   every declared key resolves; the effect iterator starts
    L-Iter     Reloading → Reloading   one iteration: a state change, its inverse, a continuation
    L-Finish   Reloading → Active      iterator exhausted, the accumulator holds every inverse
    L-Divert   Reloading → Unloading   a dependency changed mid-activation
    L-Leave    Active    → Unloading   a dependency was withdrawn, or the fiber was retired
    L-Unload   Unloading → Inactive    the accumulator runs

L-Divert is the safety rule. If a dependency changes while a component is still activating, the
fiber is diverted straight to unloading rather than finishing against a stale environment. The
effects it already applied are in the accumulator, so the rollback is complete even though the
activation was not.

Removal is deliberately two rules, not one. O-Retire only raises a flag and applies at any state;
the lifecycle rules carry the request out, through L-Leave and L-Unload, and only then may O-Remove
drop the entry. Dropping an Active fiber outright would discard its accumulator and leak.

    const fiber = ctx.use(auth, { secret })
    await fiber.dispose()   // fiber.dispose *is* the accumulator; awaiting it recovers the context

Reconfiguration is not a method on the fiber: the declarative loader owns it. The orchestrator edits
a configuration record and the loader reconciles the difference into fiber operations — for a changed
config, a dispose and a fresh ctx.use, leaving untouched entries running.

## 5. What the guarantees buy you

Recovery exactness: removing a component restores the context to a state observationally equivalent
to the one before it was added, even if other independent fibers applied their own effects in the
meantime — so the comparison is against those effects replayed, not against a frozen snapshot.
Observational, not bit-identical: what matters is that no available operation can tell the two apart.
The weakening is also the limit — each binding is restored only up to what its own key's operations
can observe, so a monotone allocator is not rewound, a heap's layout does not come back from a free,
and a message already sent stays sent.

Confluence: once the system is quiescent — every fiber settled at its target view, no transition in
flight — the state it comes to rest at is the one the same insertions and retirements would have
produced had each surviving component been loaded once, in dependency order, and none ever unloaded.
The dynamic history leaves no trace; the normal form is the statically assembled system. Two caveats:
the theorem is about the lifecycle rules alone, holding the orchestration steps fixed, and it carries
a second hypothesis, that every component is total on its provision. That different insertion orders
also land in the same place follows separately, from the set of Active fibers being determined by
which components are present and unretired and by the dependency graph, not by the schedule.

## 6. Why a TypeScript developer should care

Self-modifying agent harnesses. A harness is the runtime around a model: it composes tool suites
and execution environments, governs permissions and sandboxing, keeps session state, manages
context and memory, and orchestrates subagents. The paper's forward-looking case is a harness that
generates and deploys modifications to its own components while it is still serving requests —
model-synthesised reusable tools being the narrow precursor already in use. Every one of those
modifications is an instance of dynamic composition.

Because they land continuously and with little or no human oversight, the usual fallback stops
being viable. Without temporal composability each self-modification is a full process restart that
discards everything process-local: caches, open connections, partial computations. Rebuilding that
takes seconds to minutes. At self-modification frequency the unavailability accumulates, in-flight
tasks are disrupted over and over, and a faulty self-modification can disable the very process you
would need in order to recover from it.

Without spatial composability the failure is quieter and arrives later. Every module has to notice
for itself when a dependency appears, disappears or changes identity, and can only do so by ad hoc
means. A naive code-replacement strategy breaks dependents silently, or introduces a circular
dependency that surfaces at reload time rather than at the moment the change was made.

Why restarting the process is not the answer. Operating systems already provide temporal
composability, at the granularity of a process; container orchestrators already provide spatial
composability, at the granularity of a service. That substitute is a large part of why the problem
has attracted so little formal attention. It is not free: a restart discards accumulated state and
takes seconds to minutes to rebuild, so staying available across one means running redundant
replicas — paying in hardware for the inability to recover a single component. Container-level
orchestration cannot express a dependency between two components sharing an address space, and
pushes onto the network what could have been a local function call. Both mechanisms sit at the
process and container boundary, while the systems built on them compose at a far finer grain.

Plugin systems. Cordis (https://github.com/cordiverse) is the meta-framework behind Koishi
(https://koishi.chat/en-US/) and its 4000-plus community plugins — install, uninstall and
reconfigure live, without restarting the process. The API shown here is Cordis v4, the version the
paper describes; Koishi currently ships on v3, which shares the compositional model but differs in
the effect and coeffect semantics and in the loader.

Hot reload that cleans up. Ordinary HMR swaps the module and leaves old listeners and registry
entries behind. Effect tracking does that bookkeeping for the plugin author.

A pattern you can steal without the framework. Make every effect return its inverse, keep them on a
stack, unwind in reverse. That is the entire temporal mechanism.

## 7. Failure, and what a restart costs

The effects a component installs reach outside the context that tracks them, and a location may
refuse: a port already bound, a file that is not there, a peer that does not answer. The paper's
failure extension refines the iterator so an iteration may raise instead of yielding a triple. A raise
exits Reloading by the route of an aborting L-Divert with the premise on the target view dropped —
the iteration, not the environment, choosing the abort. The fiber routes into Unloading with the
accumulator built up to the failing iteration and arrives at Inactive having installed nothing, and the
exit writes the error on the fiber as an outcome. That outcome withholds re-entry: L-Begin is read as
requiring an error-free fiber, so a raised effect function is not retried against an unchanged
environment, and a retry has to be a revision — a reinserted fiber starts without an outcome. The
failure stays on the fiber rather than propagating to its parent, leaving siblings running. Confluence
excludes failed fibers, since whether an iteration raises depends on the state it meets.

The page closes on a bench that runs all of this at once: a harness holding a session cache and
serving requests, with a tool suite redeployed underneath it, a build that raises halfway through
activating, and — for the same change — the coarse-grained alternative of restarting the process,
which discards the cache and every other piece of process-local state.

## Limitations

An effect is revertible only where the system can modify a location exclusively and restore what was
there before. Outside that boundary an operation is untracked and acts as the identity — a direct
process.on, a mutation of somebody else's object. The boundary is drawn per location rather than per
medium, and a coeffect can move it: reifying an external location confines access to operations that
each supply an inverse. What crosses irreversibly is emission, not acquisition — open installs a
descriptor that close removes, but the bytes a write pushes through it are gone, and recovering from
those means withholding the emission or compensating for it.

On hostile code the paper is more specific than "no defence". Declared inject plus context
interception already amount to capability-style access control over proxy-mediated dependencies, and
an orchestrator can attenuate any component's access without touching the provider. But language-level
checks are moot against code that can reach the host runtime directly, so genuinely untrusted
components need an execution boundary beyond the language — a sandboxed process, a separate runtime,
a container — with the bridge appearing on the host side as an ordinary fiber.

This page is a teaching simplification; the formal content (effect iterators, observational
equivalence, the metatheory of the calculus) is in the paper.
